description: Aoyagi, Bhaskar, and Fréchette (2019) investigate how the quality of information about a partner's actions affects cooperation in a long-run strategic relationship. Participants are paired anonymously and repeatedly choose, each round, whether to cooperate or defect with their partner — earning payoffs that depend on both players' choices — knowing that the interaction may end at any moment with a fixed probability. The key manipulation is what each player learns after every round: under *perfect* monitoring, both players observe exactly what their partner did; under *public* monitoring, both receive the same noisy signal about the partner's action; and under *private* monitoring, each player receives their own noisy signal that the other cannot see — making it impossible to know whether disagreements stem from defection or bad luck. The outcome is the cooperation rate across rounds, which captures how well players sustain mutually beneficial behavior when they cannot perfectly verify each other's intentions. The original study finds that public monitoring produces meaningfully higher cooperation than private monitoring — roughly a 12-percentage-point gap — while perfect and private monitoring yield nearly identical cooperation rates, a surprising result suggesting that the *shared* nature of information, not its accuracy alone, is what enables players to coordinate punishment and sustain cooperation.

description: Dreyfuss, Heffetz, and Rabin (2022) investigate why people sometimes make seemingly irrational choices in strategy-proof mechanisms — settings where honesty is always the best strategy, no matter what others do. Participants take part in a repeated allocation game in which four prizes of different monetary values are distributed each round via a priority-based procedure: the player with the highest priority score picks first from the available prizes, then the next player picks, and so on, until all prizes are assigned. Each participant submits a rank-order list indicating their preferred ordering of the four prizes before the allocation unfolds — and because the mechanism is strategy-proof, ranking the prizes in true value order (highest to lowest) is always the dominant strategy. The outcome is whether a submitted list deviates from that truthful ranking, which captures how often participants leave money on the table by misrepresenting their preferences. The original study finds that roughly 29% of submitted lists are not the truthful ranking, and that this misrepresentation is well explained by loss aversion rooted in expectations — participants appear to form reference points based on what they anticipate receiving, making them reluctant to rank a prize highly if doing so risks the psychological pain of not getting it.

design_summary.sample_type: 72 UC Berkeley subjects from Li (2017a)'s SP-RSD treatment, organized into 18 groups of 4 players, each playing 10 rounds of random serial dictatorship. 720 subject-round observations. Each round: 4 prizes drawn uniformly without replacement from the 6-element set {$0.00, $0.25, $0.50, $0.75, $1.00, $1.25}; private priority score drawn uniformly from {1, 2, ..., 10}; 90 seconds to submit a 4-position ROL by typing 1-4 next to each prize. Allocation proceeds in priority-score order (highest first picks her top-ranked unassigned prize, etc.). $20 show-up fee plus cumulative prize winnings paid in cash at session end. Subjects received printed instructions read aloud by the experimenter (Figure 3 shows the UI; instructions reproduced p.535).

description: Chassang and Zehnder (2024) investigate how the design of internal reporting surveys affects a monitor's willingness to truthfully flag misconduct when doing so risks retaliation from the person being reported. Participants take on the role of either a monitor — someone who observes whether a paired agent has behaved badly — or an agent who can choose to punish the monitor after seeing the report. The key manipulation is the survey format: in the Direct Elicitation condition, the monitor's answer is recorded exactly as given, making it transparent who said what, while in the Hard Garbling condition, the monitor's response is passed through a randomization device that introduces plausible deniability, obscuring whether a negative report reflects the monitor's true observation or just a chance outcome. The outcome is the monitor's intended reporting decision — whether they plan to truthfully flag a bad agent — which captures how much the survey design itself can unlock honest disclosure even before retaliation actually occurs. The original study finds that Hard Garbling raises the intended reporting rate among monitors who observed bad behavior by roughly 18 percentage points compared to Direct Elicitation, a statistically significant increase suggesting that protecting reporters through deliberate ambiguity meaningfully improves the flow of sensitive information within organizations.

description: Amasino, Pace, and van der Weele (2024) investigate how a person's economic status shapes both their sense of fairness and what information they pay attention to when dividing money with others. Participants first complete a real-effort task — answering questions for pay — and are then randomly assigned to either an Advantaged role (earning more per correct answer) or a Disadvantaged role (earning less), before acting as dictators who decide how to split a joint surplus with another participant. The key manipulation is whether the dictator is Advantaged or Disadvantaged, and whether they freely choose what information to look at or are directed to focus on either merit-based information (performance scores) or outcome-based information (final earnings) before making their allocation. The outcome is the percentage of the surplus the dictator keeps for themselves, which captures how self-serving biases in attention translate into real distributional choices. The original study finds that Advantaged dictators keep substantially more of the surplus than Disadvantaged dictators — retaining around 61.5% on average compared to roughly 49.5% — and that this gap is partly explained by selective attention, as Advantaged participants dwell longer on merit information that justifies their higher earnings, while experimentally directing attention toward outcomes rather than merit causally reduces the share they allocate to themselves.

description: Fehrler and Hughes (2018) investigate how making committee deliberations publicly observable affects the quality of group decisions — specifically, whether transparency helps or hurts a committee's ability to reach the correct outcome. Participants are assigned to small committees and tasked with voting on whether to maintain a default option or switch to an alternative, after exchanging information through two structured rounds of chat: first sharing impressions of their private signal, then discussing their member type. The key manipulation is how much of the deliberation process is visible to outside observers — in the secrecy condition, internal discussions remain private, while in the transparency condition, all deliberation is publicly recorded, giving members a reason to misrepresent their private information to appear competent to outsiders. The outcome is the committee error rate — the frequency with which the group reaches the wrong decision — which captures how well the committee aggregates the private information its members hold. The original study finds that transparency significantly increases the overall rate of committee errors relative to secrecy, driven especially by a sharp rise in mistakes when the correct answer requires overturning the default, as career-concerned members strategically distort their communication rather than honestly pool their information.

description: Bigoni, Camera, and Casari (2019) investigate whether access to a monetary technology shapes people's preference for the scale of economic interaction — specifically, whether they prefer to cooperate in small, stable partnerships or large, anonymous groups. Participants play a repeated helping game in which a producer each round decides whether to give up resources to benefit a consumer, and after several cycles of play they vote on whether their next cycle should take place in a small partnership of two or a much larger group. The key manipulation is whether participants have access to tokens — an artificial currency that can be used to facilitate exchange across strangers — or must rely solely on direct reciprocity with a fixed partner; both conditions otherwise follow the same game structure and majority-rule voting procedure. The outcome is each participant's vote for the large group, which captures revealed preference for anonymous, market-like interaction over intimate, relationship-based cooperation. The original study finds that participants with access to tokens are meaningfully more likely to vote for the large group than those without — a difference of roughly 17 percentage points in individual votes during the selection phase — suggesting that monetary institutions not only enable cooperation among strangers but also make people actively choose to engage with them.

description: Charness and Sontuoso (2023) investigate how shared awareness of a decision frame affects coordination — specifically, whether knowing that others perceive the same salient features of a choice changes how people try to match each other's decisions. Participants are shown sets of three objects that differ along visual dimensions such as color, shape, and display order, and must independently choose one object with the goal of matching a partner's choice. In the Baseline condition, participants make choices without any information about what features their partner notices; in the All-Aware condition, it is made common knowledge that all players are aware of the same full set of object attributes — including the order in which objects are displayed. The outcome is the object chosen, which captures how players use salient features as focal points when trying to coordinate with a stranger. The original study finds that making full awareness common knowledge significantly increases the share of participants who choose the top-displayed object, suggesting that display order becomes a stronger focal point precisely when everyone knows everyone else can see it.

description: Calford and Cason (2024) investigate whether the timing structure of a collective-action problem — specifically, whether people decide all at once or in sequential stages — affects how well groups coordinate to provide a public good. Participants receive a private signal about their own valuation and decide whether to contribute to a shared "Group Project" or keep earnings for a "Private Project," with the group project succeeding only if enough members contribute. The key manipulation is whether the game is *static* — everyone commits simultaneously without observing others — or *dynamic* — players move in stages and can observe some teammates' choices before making their own decision, enabling them to reason conditionally about what others' actions reveal. The outcome is the rate at which the public good is successfully provided, which captures how effectively groups overcome the free-rider problem that typically undermines voluntary cooperation. The original study finds that dynamic mechanisms increase overall public-good provision relative to static mechanisms — particularly when the threshold for success is moderately or highly demanding — because observing early contributions allows later movers to update their beliefs and coordinate more effectively, even though first-stage contributions are strategically lower in the dynamic setting.
